newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia harvest seen above official forecast-trade.
newsitem.headline: Russia harvest seen above official forecast-trade.

text.p: Russia's grain harvest will probably exceed Moscow's official forecasts, making imports less likely, according to agricultural analysts.
Deputy Agriculture Minister Vladimir Alginin said by telephone the ministry was sticking to a forecast of 70 million net tonnes, barely above last year's poor 69.3 million tonnes.

But senior trade and industry sources said real output this year could be up to 15 percent higher, since the ministry figure did not account for underreporting by peasants disgruntled over painful market reforms.
Arkady Zlochevsky, president of the OGO commodities trading company, said net grain output could hit 80 million tonnes.
"Based on our analysis of per-region yields, the weather and sowings, we think this level is achievable," he said.

But Zlochevsky, who has always believed Russian farmers drastically underreport their results, said the increase would not be that significant since last year's output was really 76 million tonnes, he said, far above the official 69.3 million.

Arkady Blyumin, head of the semi-private Informzerno analytical centre, forecast output at 75-80 million tonnes. "The market and farms are flush with grain," he said, adding strong domestic supplies had pushed prices down.
"Imports aren't advantageous," he said. "You can buy cheaper here, and there's material to buy."

Russia began harvesting crops in its southern grain-belt regions this week, launching an operation which is carried out like a military invasion and involves legions of students-turned-farmers overnight.
Russian farm output has contracted a massive 40 percent since its peak levels in the Soviet era, and the past two harvests have been the worst two on record in three decades.
The state of the farm sector is still shrouded in Soviet-style suspicion and secrecy.
"A lot of grain was hidden last year," Blyumin said.

Russia's harvest is a great guessing game, since farms across this former agricultural powerhouse are spread out from St Petersburg to Siberia and almost no centralised market mechanisms are in place.

"We will not tell you what our forecast is because no one cares about the collapse of Russian agriculture," said a spokesman for the Agrarian Union, the beleaguered farm lobby's organisation. "But as any farmer will tell you, anything can happen until the grain is in the elevators."
Vasily Chinkaryov, deputy chief executive of importers Eximkhleb, said crops would recover and imports were not needed.

"Look at how many years we've gotten by without big imports -- a lot," he said, referring to the fact the government was no longer a grain importer. "There will be some buying here and there but it will be from Ukraine and Kazakshtan."
A trader at a Western commodities house forecast the 1997 harvest at 75 million tonnes or so and also ruled out any large-scale imports from the United States or Europe.

"There might be some prompt shipments of five or ten thousand tonnes here and there but there won't be a return to the past," he said, referring to Soviet-era Moscow's massive, multi-million tonnes raids on world wheat markets in the 1970s.
But Russian sources said farmers were offering to sell feed grains but no milling wheat -- a sign that high-quality bread making wheat could be in short supply.

"Practically everywhere, the weather is good," said the trader. But he added, "One of the major problems for Russia is quality. Until the harvest is over, nobody can really say what the situation will be."

Blyumin estimated domestic grain prices, already at or above world levels, would reverse the previous years' trend and not rise in 1997. Grain prices skyrocketed 210 percent in 1995 and 370 percent in 1996 before slowing to 30 percent last year.
